World.title: ‘Still Kelly country’: Life in Porepunkah after Dezi Freeman, as locals pick up the pieces
World.content:
It was those tactical police, with their big guns, who told Kompe that Freeman had shot and killed two police officers and injured another when they’d gone to his home to serve a warrant in a child sexual abuse investigation. Freeman, 56, had stolen a police pistol and vanished into the trees down by the Buckland River, and he was still on the run.

Almost a year ago, on another misty day like this, it was the police who came checking on Kompe. They were looking for a man he once knew well. Kompe first met Desmond Filby down by this river in the 1980s, and began teaching the long-haired teenager bushcraft. Forty years on, Filby was living in his own solar-powered retreat, off-grid, just a few kilometres up the hill, but he had taken a new name: Dezi Freeman.

Ray Kompe, who knew Dezi Freeman, at his off-the-grid hut in the Buckland Valley. “I’m a bit of a recluse these days,” he says.

When we arrive, the former gold prospector has just hoisted a huge new lithium battery onto the roof. It weighs more than he does. “The neighbours did have to check I hadn’t done myself in,” grins Kompe. He emerges from behind his little hut’s screen door with a torch still aglow on his beanie and the sleepy look of a miner stumbling back into the light.

It was built more than a century ago in Victoria’s high country, so close to the Buckland River in Porepunkah that you can hear the water rushing past under the wind. Back then, that river still gave up lumps of gold like Easter eggs. But today, you might think the hut long abandoned, if not for the patchwork of solar panels wired along its roof. They were put there – using an elaborate “Batman-style” abseiling rig – by its reclusive yet nimble 73-year-old inhabitant, Ray Kompe.

There is a little hut at the foot of the mountain, just minutes down the road from where Australia’s biggest-ever manhunt began.

Well before COVID, though, Kompe had had enough of Dezi. “He fell in with that conspiracy crowd. He was watching these violent WWII videos … of Japanese torture. Sickening stuff. I just thought: ‘Why am I here with this weirdo?’ ”

“Well, he wouldn’t be welcome here any more,” says Kompe. For decades, he’d put up with his fixations, his rants against the government, as they explored the bush and its hidden mineshafts and waterfalls together. But the idealistic teenager who loved photography and attended hippie festivals had undeniably grown into a bitter and angry man. Even before the pandemic, he’d become a fanatical adherent of the pseudo-law peddled by so-called “ sovereign citizens ”, those who don’t recognise the authority of government – who drive under fake licence plates and change their names to Freeman (free man).

Inside Kompe’s hut, we squeeze past a bicycle in the hall and a shower in the kitchen. He apologises for the mess while his white chihuahua Luna darts around our ankles. Kompe watched the police comb through it all a year ago – the start of hundreds of raids on properties across the high country in search of Freeman and those who helped him. They flew a tiny drone “the size of two cigarette packets” straight through his place, politely weaving between towers of books and cassette tapes, into cupboards. Officers even shone a light down into the outside dunny. No Freeman.

I’ve come to see Kompe because I’m trying to understand how someone could survive in the wild here – or at least how they could be smuggled out of it under the noses of what felt to locals at times like half the state’s police force. But then there’s so much more to understand about what happened in Porepunkah than that, especially for the families still mourning and the remote community still divided by the violence at its door.

It would be another seven months before police caught sight of him again – when he emerged, wrapped in a doona, from a shipping container at a remote hideout more than 100 kilometres away near the NSW border. After a three-hour standoff, Freeman dropped the doona to fire that stolen revolver and was shot dead by the tactical snipers calling for his surrender.

Them meaning the “cookers”, the sovereign citizens – especially the ones who hate being called sovereign citizens. “You know, the nutjobs,” says Wendt.

Thompson also knew Freeman. He’d gone along with the other nine officers serving the warrant that day because it was hoped that he might be able to reason with the conspiracy theorist. He’d spoken of Freeman in the weeks prior, Thompson’s best friends Andrew “Crouchy” Crouch and Dirk Wendt tell me over a beer back in Melbourne. “Thommo was thinking: ‘We’ll sort it. I’ll talk him down again,’ ” says Crouch. “I didn’t realise then how big a stronghold that area’s become for them.”

Detective Thompson, known as “Thommo”, knew this country well, and how treacherous it can be beyond the tourist bubble of Bright. This is not the Australian bush as seen in dusty, outback noir: stray from the path and the scrub is thick and wet, threaded with blackberries and secret tunnels. Riverbanks can suddenly burst and turn whole clearings into marshlands.

Neal Thompson (left) and Vadim de Waart-Hottart (pictured with a painting done for him by someone he helped through a mental health crisis) were remembered as adventurous and kind. “Thommo” was known for his silly Macgyver fixes out bush, but singular focus on the job. And both he and de Waart-Hottart (“the romantic”) were still adored as family by their former partners.

Those who knew the two officers killed – including local police not authorised to speak publicly ahead of an inquest into the deaths – say problems between police and the “cookers” in the hills had been brewing before the shooting. “But we didn’t know what we were walking into,” says an officer who was there when it happened.

The night Freeman murdered seasoned local detective Neal Thompson, 59, and 35-year-old rising star, Vadim de Waart-Hottart, snow fell on Mount Buffalo. A battering blizzard of rain and lightning howled down the spine of the tourist road as scores of heavily armed police scoured the forest for the fugitive.

Instead, that Tuesday, Crouchy heard news of the Porepunkah killings over the police radios. Thommo, his best friend since he was 12, the cop who was always first through the door, had been shot dead. Crouch’s unit, the dog squad, was called up to the high country to hunt for the killer.

“He was finding it harder than I expected, harder than I did, giving it up,” says Crouch. “But we had real adventures planned for retirement.”

Secretly, though, he was chuffed. And a little overwhelmed. He’d joined the force barely out of his teens and he liked the swagger it gave him around town. He liked helping people. He still wore the same long, black detective’s coat he’d always worn, chasing crooks through wheatfields, crashing police cars, as if he’d rocketed straight out of a 1980s cop drama. His favourite crook in town called him “The Don”.

Thommo and Crouchy were supposed to retire together. Two cops working at opposite ends of Victoria, they’d grown up together in Bendigo, and now they’d lined up their final shifts to fall within days of each other. Thommo always had to be first through the door, “like a bull at the gate”, Crouch says, so, of course, Thommo was retiring first, too. A party was planned that Friday, though Thommo was worried his station in Wangaratta would do a guard of honour “or some nonsense”, and had a sly idea to nip off to the pub early.

When I arrive in Bright on the first night of the town’s popular winter festival, my accommodation host explains: “People come here for the peace. But some people come here to hide. Especially out there. Who are you here with again?”

This March, his parents returned to Australia and to the same police chapel to commemorate the Russell Street bombings that killed another young officer in Melbourne 40 years ago. Beside them was Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush, as he had been during Vadim’s funeral.

It rained for days after the Porepunkah murders, every day for nearly a fortnight. But, on September 5, the day of de Waart-Hottart’s funeral, the sun broke through the stained-glass windows of the police academy chapel in Melbourne, as the young constable was being laid to rest. His mother Carolina smiled, raising her hands to the light. She’d told those gathered at the funeral that her son would live on in nature, and now here he was, her Vadim, making everyone smile again.

The lobby was packed full of flowers and tributes for de Waart-Hottart and Thompson at the Wangaratta police station in the weeks after the shooting.

“We’ll have to clear all this out soon,” says Vogels, staring at the photographs of Thompson and de Waart-Hottart still on display on the little white table in the foyer, children’s drawings pinned to the wall behind. “We’re going to do something special for them.”

A permanent memorial is now being hewn out of rock outside the station for Thompson alongside de Waart-Hottart – the “gentle giant” from Belgium who had been excited to explore the Alpine wilds on his new secondment from Melbourne. A female officer, who narrowly escaped the shooting herself when the homemade shotgun Freeman turned on her jammed, has been fundraising with her son for a similar memorial outside the Bright station, ahead of Victoria Police commemorations on August 26.

At Wangaratta police station in those early days, there were so many flowers piled in the entryway, the doors could barely close, says Senior Sergeant Luke Vogels. People brought slabs of beer too, though sadly, policy dictated the tinnies had to be turned away. Nothing like this had ever really happened before.

He couldn’t tell them then, but, while they gathered, officers were analysing surprise new intelligence about the whereabouts of their son’s killer. Detectives had thought Freeman already dead – months of searching had failed to turn up a single, useful lead. Now suddenly they had one, and it led to a remote property in the state’s north.

De Waart-Hottart’s mother and brother at his funeral (left), and Andrew Crouch helping carry Thompson’s coffin during his service days later in September 2025. Eddie Jim; Justin McManus

Three days later, when Freeman was found there and shot dead, de Waart-Hottart’s parents were the first people Bush called. Today, police are piecing together how he got there, and who they believe helped him. Multiple people have been raided and arrested. No one has yet been charged.

But “sov-cit” ideas are growing in these hills and beyond, locals say. All elections, from councils to federal parliament, have seen an increase in sov-cit protest votes. Even some of Thommo’s friends, people he got to know out hunting and fishing, would later turn out to be sympathetic to Freeman’s anti-government cause, as conspiracy theorists lionised the fugitive online. They called Freeman the modern-day Ned Kelly. Porepunkah is, after all, they said, just 80 kilometres from Glenrowan, where Kelly made his last stand against police 150-odd years ago.

“This is still Kelly country,” says Freeman’s close friend, Bruce Evans, adjusting a velcro strap on his camouflage pants. It’s a common refrain.

Bruce Evans says he misses his good mate Dezi Freeman, but adds: “I know he shot those cops.” Jason South

In Bright, where the hills cast shadows of green velvet, the murders split the community. Some rallied around Freeman’s Filipino wife Mali, well-liked but left homeless and adrift with their children after he fled. Others tied blue ribbons to lamp poles to honour the officers shot.

Leanne Boyd, who once employed Mali at her popular cafe and helped fundraise supplies for her, says she fell somewhere in the middle. She was no fan of her friend Mali’s odd husband, but the strain of people pulling in both directions left her exhausted. Either Freeman was a monster or an outlaw hero. Either Mali was his Lady Macbeth accomplice or “a f---ing saint”, as one friend of Freeman’s hisses at me down the phoneline.

It’s the morning rush at Boyd’s cafe and a pen wobbles in her long, blonde hair; a tremulous, load-bearing look about it. These days Mali is rarely seen around town, though prosecutors have dropped talk of charging her over the shootings. “Mali always asks, ‘What’s going on in the outside world?’ ” sighs Boyd. “She just wants peace. I think we’re all sick of thinking about it.”

Leanne Boyd says “the kindness came from everywhere at first” as locals rallied around police – and Freeman’s young family left behind – after the shootings. Jason South

I understand. Four months ago, when Freeman was shot dead, I’d driven up this mountain and stood on this street and asked the same questions. One in a parade of journalists periodically crashing over the town like the tide and then retreating, with business cards tucked in the crooks of doors and letterboxes. Bright had been all bustling colour then, orange leaves trodden underfoot in the final hours of the Easter weekend. There was hope that, with Freeman gone, the tourism that powered the town would come roaring back to life.

Some businesses are still recovering from the manhunt lockdown that choked off the rare, bumper snow season of 2025, even with government assistance grants. Boyd says she lost $28,000, back when her only customers were the undercover cops in town (“They dressed too well to be locals or ski bunnies”).

“Magic town”: tourists and locals enjoy the start of Winter Fest in Bright in late July. Jason South

Still, today there is fake snow on the air, and fairy-lights overhead and the town is once again heaving with out-of-towners for the winter festival. Over Boyd’s shoulder, I watch a couple struggling to fit armfuls of hire skis – and their gigantic, grinning Samoyed – into the back of a hatchback.

Only the year before the shooting, the property that borders the farm where it happened was taken over by a film crew for production of Netflix movie War Machine. “People with guns were running around then, too, fighting imaginary aliens,” says local Gary Monshing. “So we’ve had a bit on around here.”

Gary’s daughter Georgia and her partner Ben now run the family ski gear shop in Porepunkah. It’s one of many competing ski shops on the tourist road – at least two of them guarded by near-identical border collies – and the Monshings are exactly the kind of genuine, postcard-friendly people that make tourism agencies breathless to remind the public that, yes, Bright really is the same honey-gold snow town it’s always been, thank you very much.

Georgia Monshing and Ben Kaye (pictured with their daughter Milla) didn’t want to complain about the manhunt lockdown choking off business (though they made a good trade in snowchains for police cars), but say they are relieved the area’s now bouncing back. Jason South

But while many locals are eager not to be defined by the tragedy, others seem just as eager to stress that they don’t believe “the official story”. Some trust police even less than before. And the question of who helped Freeman on the run – and who might have helped turn him in – is still there too, on the air.

When Freeman was killed in March, his eldest son posted a plea online for people not to celebrate. “That’s still my father,” Koah wrote.

Josh Roose, a researcher who advises police and governments on extremism cases, calls the high country “strange country”, where the modern, online phenomenon of sov-cits collides with old bush mythology of the outlaw. You’ll find people in rural poverty, off-grid in makeshift shelters or huts like Kompe – once living rough by the river and still hesitant to use the heating until after dark, until it’s really cold – while, next door, luxury Airbnbs sit empty half the year.

As police hunted Freeman, drones buzzed in the night, but properties were too vast to properly surveil, and phone taps quiet. (“Everyone knew they were listening,” says Boyd.) Some locals even refused to serve police coffee, Roose recalls. “It’s a closed shop up there. They might get tourists but the locals are the locals. That’s their defining borderline between us and them.”

The thing to remember about the Freeman case, Roose tells me, is that “Dezi was not only deeply embedded in a network of anti-government types” – though he was, he was up to his neck in them the way you can find yourself up to your neck in blackberries in the scrub. But Freeman was also “just embedded in his local community in a way most people don’t understand”.

When the sun sets behind the mountain, an underground network of two-way radios crackle to life. Among those listening is Bright blacksmith (and one-time bikie) Stephen Mallett. As the head of Australia’s main “doomsday prepper” Facebook community, he’s met many of those at the other end of the line. Sometimes it’s someone on the roads needing help. Sometimes it’s someone like Freeman. Mallett knew him before the shooting as another local preparing for catastrophe – whatever flavour of civil war, foreign invasion or asteroid collision you preferred. “But the day of the shootings,” says Mallett, “the radio waves all went dead.”

He was one of the first of Freeman’s associates raided (and cleared of helping him). When he opened his door in the howling rain to find red lasers pointed at his chest, he considered racing for his back fence and the forest behind – that forest of old mines, forgotten huts and hidden waterfalls. Mallett is perhaps the 20th local to tell me that police, in their months of searching, didn’t cover even half of it. But Mallett didn’t run.

Stephen Mallet, pictured with his dog Tucker. Eddie Jim

“Nothing to hide. And I was afraid they’d shoot my dog,” he says as he shows me his camouflage “bug-out bag” or emergency pack. The thing to grab in case of apocalypse. He wouldn’t take the huge knives he makes, custom, for “hippie chicks” online if he was running. He’d pack light. And he’d keep moving, through the pine plantations, the wineries, stealing off fruit trees or going up the waters Freeman used to kayak, which all rush north to the Murray River, near where he was discovered. “They’d never find you.”

Friends remember Freeman pointing out his prepper stashes on the mountain and disappearing into its trees for weeks at a time to hunt. Beth Knights says he knew how to live off the land even back in their 20s, when they met at the hippie festivals in these hills, cooking over campfires and swimming naked in the river. He still went by his family name Filby then, and his hair was long. There was no electricity for a bush-doof rave, but there was a magic idealism on the air; people coming together in little tribes.

Freeman wasn’t like the city folk with whom Knights hitched a ride from Melbourne. He was a local, “with a thick, bogan accent”, but warm and fun and generous then. He knew how to build a fire break, and he’d catch fish with his hands from the river, the water coursing past his legs. Life went rushing on, of course, as it does, and dragged them apart. Knights, today a TV writer in Castlemaine, wonders what dragged Freeman under. A particular conspiracy? A personal tragedy?

Dezi Freeman (right) at a Rainbow Gathering hippie festival in the hills in the 1990s.

She remembers a bitterness in Freeman when she saw him again, at a music festival in the 2000s. “Or maybe it was just sadness. It’s like he couldn’t fit anywhere. He only made sense out there.” Something about him left an impression, though. “I always wanted to know where he ended up. I was just horrified when I realised it was him.”

For the Filbys, Freeman’s ravings had been a problem without a satisfying explanation for years. He lived off welfare support while hating the government; he made fun of “flat-earther” conspiracists, while his own biblical delusions intensified. Freeman had been deeply affected by a series of deaths in his family, though most of the Filbys left were estranged from him by the shootings, including nephews Luke and Joe. Luke remembers his uncle destroying cassettes of Metallica, once his favourite band, because he’d declared them satanic. “Dez was always the oddball uncle,” says Joe. But he was also the uncle who took a young Joe hiking when he was depressed in his teens and offered support. “We never saw anything like this coming. It’s been devastating.”

Around the time of COVID, Freeman’s attempts to arrest a local magistrate and help privately prosecute then-premier Daniel Andrews made him infamous.

But by August 2025, he was facing serious allegations of child sexual abuse, and his brother and wife finally convinced him to see a psychologist. He had an appointment booked on the day of the shooting. He never made it.

The track that leads to the Porepunkah property where Freeman shot dead the police officers. Eddie Jim

Ten minutes out of town, the old, converted bus where the Freemans lived is still there. It sits in one corner of a sprawling chestnut farm, next to the Buckland River. Under the tarp of Freeman’s makeshift kitchen, he hung a sign for the Buckland and a picture of the Virgin Mary.

You can see the property from the hills near the airfield, but it’s easy to miss the turn-off – a narrow gravel track through a tunnel of forest with a metal gate at the end. Exclusion zone, warns a handwritten, cardboard sign. No trespass. There is a strange, fairy-tale feeling to the trees here; lit gold in the sunlight, but, as the sky darkens, they lean too close.

The converted bus and living space where the Freemans lived, in one corner of the Swift farm. Jason South

Freeman’s landlords, Andrew and Rebecca Swift, still live behind this gate, in a red-roofed farmhouse with their daughters. Others live here too, “a little community”, according to neighbours and friends. But few people get past the gate.

Freeman made it himself, an elaborate early-warning system of security codes and solar-powered cameras, with more hidden throughout the trees. He always had eyes in the bush, locals say. He’d construct elaborate “hides” from which to watch his neighbours, strap cameras to his chest and don camouflage suits that made him look like Chewbacca. When child services and police surrounded the bus more than once in the years before the shooting – out of concern for the Freeman children – their approach was picked up by this ring of CCTV.

The Swifts aren’t answering the phone, but the gate’s warnings grow more strident the further I read. Offenders will be prosecuted and fined a minimum of ten thousand dollars.

They’re well-liked in town, the Swifts, though fiercely private. Rebecca in particular is known for her anti-government views. The Freemans moved onto their farm four years ago, after a string of fallings-out between Freeman and his former landlords had left them homeless. People speak of Freeman’s terrifying temper, of his obsession with guns and a mysterious marijuana crop that sprung up at one property in Myrtleford. Most of all, Freeman hated female cops. But the shootings in August caught the Swifts by surprise. “They’re peaceful people,” says friend Bruce Evans.

Police had decided a specialist sniper squad wasn’t needed that day to serve the warrant, hoping to keep Freeman calm. Instead, they sent 10 officers, including two of their best: Thompson the veteran and de Waart-Hottart, formerly of the city’s public order response unit.

In Andrew Swift’s own account of what unfolded when Freeman barricaded himself in the bus with Mali and their toddler – as told to a YouTuber who runs wellness festivals, not “the mainstream media” – Swift says he never heard Freeman warn police he had a gun.

Freeman shot Thompson first as the detective climbed in through the bus window. Then de Waart-Hottart.

A preliminary hearing for the upcoming inquest heard that Freeman stole de Waart-Hottart’s gun and used it to shoot Thompson a second time, where he lay on the ground. “Can you hear us Thommo?” called one of the other officers now taking cover. “F---ing scum, die in hell,” said Freeman.

At Thommo’s favourite cafe, run by close friend Anita Cook, a plaque by one bench now reads “Neal’s corner”. “He was kind of the man in my life that I depended on,” says Cook, who saw Thompson as usual when he stopped by before work the day of the shooting. “He’d always sneak in early to surprise me. I’ve only just stopped looking up expecting to see him.” Jason South

Roose gave expert testimony at the inquest into the 2022 Wieambilla shootings – when Christian extremists murdered two police officers and a neighbour at a remote Queensland property. That should have been a routine missing-person check. But, like Freeman, the Train family hated police, and called them “devils”.

Since the Porepunkah shootings, Freeman’s image has started appearing on posters at far-right rallies throughout Australian cities. Yet, in the regions where these ideologies are also brewing, mental health services and other supports remain painfully thin, says Roose – a knife’s edge. “We have to wake up to this as a serious threat.”

Sunday in Bright, and under the soaring timber beams of the Our Lady of the Snows church, Father Tony Shallue is delivering a sermon on the dangers of misinformation. The Freemans came here most Sundays, including two days before the shooting, though Father Tony worried about Freeman’s strange slide into doomsday fanaticism, his ravings about the Antichrist.

“In this world of information, not all of it is wisdom,” the priest tells his flock now. It’s a sermon so on theme I wonder if my cover is already blown, having just strolled in off the street to find the congregation in a late Mass. The singing had drawn me in. A black dog is tied up out front.

Father Tony briefly pauses his sermon warning of technology coming between people to wrestle with a malfunctioning microphone. But it’s not all bad, he continues, if it brings us together.

The main farmhouse at the Porepunkah property where the shooting happened, pictured during the manhunt. Joe Armao

We check back on Ray Kompe at his hut, where the only real technology is the solar panels and the gadgets he fashions himself. Kompe apologises again for the mess, but the closer I look, the more I sense an order to the clutter. His dog’s vet records hang, neatly labelled, on one wall. On another are framed drawings from his neighbours’ children, the neighbours who check on him.

People tried to check on Freeman, when they knew something had taken him under. Others seemed happy to draw him deeper and deeper into the whirlpool of pseudo law and conspiracies.

In the past year, Kompe says he’s lost interest in making gadgets entirely, though he’s not sure why. “Everyone’s just on their phones now,” he offers, half-heartedly, but he’s looking across the field, towards the hill where the boy he knew as Desmond Filby shot three men.

“I mean, the world doesn’t ever really go away, does it?”

World.title: The 54 Nurses: dodgy stats and the real health workforce data
World.content:
This week the Minister of Health was forced into an admission that threatens the wider government narrative of success in Health.

We look at the admission and look across nine years of nursing workforce data. Just how many nurses have been added, when, and by whom?

54 nurses: A grudging admission and the data on nurses The House Download MP3 5m

"Yes" - so hard to say

Wednesday's Question Time ended a week's long struggle when Labour's Ayesha Verrall forced a single reluctant word from the Minister of Health, Simeon Brown - "Yes".

The question repeatedly sidestepped was "Is it correct that the net increase in Health New Zealand full-time equivalent nursing staff between the quarters ending March 2024 and March 2026 is 54?"

When the "yes" finally came, the House dissolved into groans of "was that so hard?" and "caught in a lie".

Adding 54 extra nurses across two years is contrary to an oft-repeated Government mantra; that more than 2,000 extra nurses have been added by the Government. It is held up as key evidence of success.

Minutes earlier, the Prime Minister wielded the number to bat away questions about nurse safety. "I can tell the member they certainly appreciate having 2,100 more nurses in the system than when we came to Government."

The background data

We referred to the data sets that Simeon Brown referred to in his non-answers - Health New Zealand's Workforce Information Programme, which thankfully has largely kept the same categories and time frames across multiple governments (and is easily accessible back to 2016).

There are four background factors to note: Total workforce counts, turnover, the quarterly snapshot, and the duration of the hiring process.

First: There are a lot of nurses in the public health system, though apparently not as many as are required. The latest count is 35,342 individual nurses, but some are part-time, so the most accurate comparison is the number of Full Time Equivalents (FTE), currently 29,458.

That number is from a July update to the most recent quarterly report (to end of March 2026). The report notes that the data is a snapshot taken at 31 March 2026. What was changed for the July update is not clearly specified.

Second: Nursing turnover has ranged in recent years from about 8 percent to 13 percent annually. On average, that turnover requires 3,500 nurses (3,000 FTE) to be hired each year just to keep numbers static.

Politicians commonly clarion that they are 'currently advertising for thousands of nurses', which sounds impressive but if thousands of nurses are not hired every year, total nursing numbers will slip quickly.

Three: Staffing counts are quarterly. The snapshots are for the final day of each March, June, September and December. Counting does not start afresh when the government changes.

Four: Hiring is not an instant process (especially within a bureaucracy, and more so when budgets are tight). A new hire will typically involve a business case, various approvals of the plan to recruit, the advertising of vacancies and winnowing of applications, interviews, reference checks, and then waiting for successful applicants to become available after giving notice elsewhere.

In a best case scenario the process might take two to three months, but in reality it can take much longer, as RNZ's Ruth Hill reported in late 2025: "Hospitals in the Wellington region are waiting up to six months for Health NZ to give them approval to even begin recruitment for front-line roles."

The quarterly snapshots and hiring lags make it very difficult to definitively credit any one government with rises or falls that occur near a change of government.

Nurses and supporters protest at Waikato Hospital, Hamilton, 30 July 2025. Libby Kirkby-McLeod

Is it 2,100 extra nurses or 54?

Here are the full-time equivalent counts of nurses across the last eight years.

On 31 December 2017, two months after Jacinda Ardern's first coalition was sworn in (October 26), the snapshot counted 21,918 nurses.

On 31 December 2020, soon after the second Labour-led government was sworn in (November 6) there were 24,552 nurses.

Across those three years the number of nurses rose by 2,634 - an increase of 12 percent.

On 31 December 2023, a month after National were sworn in (November 27) there were 28,206 nurses.

Across those three years the number of nurses rose by 3,654 - an increase of 14.9 percent.

The most recent data is the July update on the 31 March 2026 workforce snapshot. It counts 29,458 nurses.

Across those 2 ½ years the number of nurses has increased by 1,252 - an increase so far of 4.4 percent.

A 4.4 percent increase is positive, but only roughly a third of the rises in either of the two previous government terms. That may still rise by the equivalent 31 December snapshot.

If the current Government wanted to beat Labour's 14.9 percent nursing rise, it could ignore nursing and focus on a different snapshot staffing category.

Either 'Midwives' (a 23 percent increase with the addition of 248 midwives) or 'Corporate and Other' (a 16.5 percent increase with the addition of 2,488 new corporate staff), though that second one might be less popular.

Where do the numbers 54 and 2,100 come from?

A reason for the very grudging answer from Minister of Health Simeon Brown is that it highlights that all but 54 of the 1,252 extra nurses added since December 2023 were already on staff when the 31 March 2024 snapshot was counted - by the end of the Government's first four months in office. Presumably their arrival occurred after a long and bureaucratic employment process that started who knows when.

The higher 2,100 number appears to have been achieved by stretching reality to its statistical limits. Reaching 2100 requires two imaginative leaps. Firstly, you must count all part time nurses as a whole unit (ignoring the more accurate Equivalent Full Time method). Secondly you have to imagine that the current government were making hiring decisions prior to even winning the 2023 election.

2,162 is the difference in the non-EFT nurse count between 30 September 2023 and the latest 2026 snapshot. 30 September is two weeks prior to the 2023 election and two months before Christopher Luxon's administration was even sworn in.

Hell is statistics

Sadly, the truth is that you cannot trust any statistics heard in Parliament's debating chamber - from anyone. They may be true or they may be balderdash, but either way, they are almost certainly misleading. It is a fact that all statistics are ripe for manipulation.

Oppositions won't highlight government successes, though there are always some. Governments won't highlight their own failures, though these too are guaranteed.

At any one time some categories will be up, others down. If total staffing numbers are bad, the answer is to highlight a region, or shift the comparative time period, or focus on a different category. For example, while the increase in nurses has been low since March 2024, the number of doctors has been higher. If all else fails, only count the things that you can control, like the number of people on waiting lists.

This is just as true outside health. If violent crime is up, the answer is to focus on property crime (which tends to have an inverse correlation and is likely to be down).

The public airing and discussion of both favourable and unfavorable information is a key purpose of Question Time, and of Parliament. Governments get to share good news stories via patsy questions, but oppositions must also be able to raise issues and receive real responses. When oppositions struggle to get responses, incorrect claims can gain footholds and over time grow harder to walk back, becoming a story in themselves.

World.title: Weather: Heavy rain warnings for South Island, severe gales to batter lower North Island
World.content:
Heavy rain is expected to hit southern regions over the weekend.

MetService said western areas of the South Island were likely to get heavy rain on Saturday.

Severe gales would follow on Sunday, while snow would fall in Otago and high-altitude roads across the South Island.

"A series of fronts, embedded within a strong and moist northwest flow, move over New Zealand today and tomorrow, followed by a change to strong, colder southwesterlies," the forecaster said on Saturday morning, urging people to keep up to date.

A heavy rain watch was issued for Westland and areas south of Aoraki/Mt Cook, lasting from 9am Saturday to 9am Sunday. Thunderstorms were possible, with a moderate chance of upgrading to a warning.

Orange strong wind warnings were also in place for Tararua District, Wairarapa, Wellington and Marlborough Sounds for Sunday morning.

A heavy snow watch will be in place for Southern Lakes and Central Otago from 5am to 4pm Sunday, above 700m, with a moderate chance of upgrading to a warning.

And MetService said strong wind was possible for inland Hawke's Bay about and south of State Highway 5 between 8am and 2pm Sunday; and in Marlborough about and east of the Kaikoura ranges between 7am and 3pm Sunday.

World.title: Fleeing driver in Palmerston North leaves officer in critical condition
World.content:
A police officer is in a critical condition after being hit by a fleeing driver in Palmerston North overnight.

Superintendent Dion Bennett said the driver had been signalled to stop about 2am on Amberley Avenue but allegedly fled.

"Minutes later, the vehicle, which was not being pursued, hit a Police officer laying spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road.

"The officer suffered critical injuries and was airlifted to Wellington Hospital, while a second officer was treated for minor injuries."

Bennett said the vehicle's two occupants were both young people and had been arrested at the scene.

Police Minister Mark Mitchell told RNZ he was travelling to Wellington to support the injured officer.

"The Commissioner and I will be providing any support that the family require," he said.

"Policing by its sheer nature does carry risk, there's no doubt about that, but of course that doesn't lessen or reduce the impact that is felt when one of our police officers is injured in the line of duty.

"They are out there protecting their community, they are representative of us, they do carry that risk, but it doesn't make it any easier when a police officer is seriously hurt, injured or killed."

The president of the Police Association, Steve Watt, said incidents like this were felt by all members.

"Ultimately, the police is a big family and when these sorts of things happen it really cuts deep and it affects us all," he said.

"Much like the rest of our members, we're waiting and hoping for the best outcome."

Watt said they were working with police's welfare network and organising wrap around support not only for the officer but for his family.

"There's a reasonably large contingent of family that have headed to Wellington, so we'll look to continue to support them and make sure that they're well looked after," he said.

A scene examination was carried out by the Serious Crash Unit and a section of the road remains closed.

A Police Critical Incident Investigation had been launched, and police said they are trying to understand the full circumstances of what occurred and notify relevant agencies.

"This work will take time, and we will share information when we are in a position to do so," Bennett said.

"In the meantime, we are wrapping support around the staff members involved and their whānau, as well as their colleagues."

Echoes of previous case

The injuring of the Palmerston North officer comes 18 years after Sergeant Derek Wootton was killed while laying road spikes in Porirua, north of Wellington.

The 52-year-old was working the night shift when a report was received of a serious assault and carjacking.

Police patrols saw the reported stolen Honda near Porirua and followed it to Titahi Bay. The Honda had reached speeds of 160km/h as it drove through residential streets. Wootton was struck by the car as he deployed the spikes at around 3am on Dimock Street in Titahi Bay. The impact propelled him nearly 30m down the road.

Wootton had previously worked as a builder and milkman before joining the police, and was first posted to Porirua as a constable when he graduated in 1994. Then-Wellington Police District Commander Pieri Munroe described him as an experienced frontline supervisor.

Andrew Popo, a 32-year-old Mongrel Mob member, was charged with dangerous driving, dangerous driving causing death and failing to stop after a motor accident. He was also charged with aggravated robbery, the theft of a Honda Prelude and kidnapping a 16-year-old. He was sentenced to eight years and nine months in jail for manslaughter.

Justice McKenzie says he took into account Popo's genuine remorse and his guilty plea to the manslaughter charge, but also noted a previous history of offending and gang connections.

World.title: The Cleary theories: Could Nathan really come to the Warriors?
World.content:
Analysis: Speculation of where Nathan Cleary will play beyond Penrith 2027 has ramped up in recent weeks, with the superstar halfback yet to confirm his plans when his contract expires at the Panthers.

The Warriors have long been linked with the Auckland-raised premiership-winner, whose father Ivan Cleary coached the club for seven seasons before a shift to the Panthers in 2012, and it's no secret fans would love to see Nathan call Mt Smart home.

In fact, speculation of a trans-Tasman move recently grew so intense that Nathan addressed it publicly at a press conference, saying he would not want to come to Auckland and stand in the way of his younger brother Jett - a halfback for the Warriors who is yet to make his first-grade debut.

But the Warriors are far from the only club in the conversation and there are also whispers of a move to the NRL's newest club, the PNG Chiefs, while a potentially radical move to the UK Super League has also been floated.

Now, with Jett having been granted an early release from the Warriors to return to Australia, some pundits are saying the door to Mt Smart could be opening wider for Nathan.

Here are just a few of the theories for where Nathan might end up:

1 November 2026. Mark the date in your calendars.

Code Sports journalist Dean Ritchie says all signs point to Nathan starting talks with rival clubs from November 1 - and there's a whole lot of interested parties chasing him with open cheque books.

"I keep hearing from very good sources and I'll repeat myself, I'm told he is going to go to November 1."

Speaking on NRL360 this week, Ritchie indicated the Warriors were increasingly shaping as the Panthers' most formidable rival in securing Nathan's signature.

"I don't know where he's going to end up, but I keep hearing that a viable option is the Warriors," he said.

"It never left the frame."

A young Nathan Cleary supporting the Warriors in 2010. Anthony Au-Yeung

Asked last month - before Jett's request for an early release - whether he was any closer to making a call on his future, Nathan had said he was "still in the process of thinking it over".

"I wasn't born in Auckland, but I grew up a fair bit there and I will admit I was a Warriors fan growing up."

He added that at the end of the day, "even if that was an option, I'd be blocking my little brother's pathway. I'm not too sure about that".

Could Jett's departure change things?

The reserved #7 step

The NRL's 19th team, the PNG Chiefs, are building a world-class roster ahead of their planned entry into the competition in 2028, having already secured several high-profile players including Nathan's former Penrith teammates Jarome Luai and Brian To'o, along with all-time leading try-scorer Alex Johnston and NSW State of Origin representative Zac Lomax.

The club has also signed Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson and English forward Matty Lees.

The stairwell leading to the Chiefs' interim offices inside Port Moresby's National Football Stadium showcases its top-30 recruits, engraved on individual steps by order of arrival.

Every player to date has been allocated a number (though that does not necessarily correspond to their on-field role).

The seventh step is marked "007 (reserved)".

Is the club's choice to keep that number vacant hinting at a potential halfback signing? Could Nathan be the Chiefs' final marquee player?

Speaking on SEN radio, former premiership winner Matty Johns said his sources are confident PNG will sign either Nathan, or current Roosters halfback Sam Walker.

"The money (at PNG) is crazy," he said.

"Apparently, they're very confident. My mail is they're confident that they'll get either Cleary or Walker. That's what they're talking."

Nathan and Jett Cleary NRL

London Calling?

Another possible scenario for Nathan may be a move to London.

How? It is slightly complicated, but perhaps not as far-fetched as a move to Mt Smart.

While Cleary would attract plenty of interest from NRL clubs, Johns believes his future could be in the Northern Hemisphere - with girlfriend and Manchester City football star Mary Fowler a significant drawcard.

Last week, the NRL made a bid to buy Super League, the struggling UK counterpart to Australasia's professional rugby league competition.

The proposal centres on the idea that an NRL takeover could revive a competition that has struggled since the late 1990s, while strengthening and expanding rugby league's overall global footprint.

At the same time, Australian rugby league great Darren Lockyer has recently bought and revamped the London Broncos, who currently play in the second tier of the English competition.

Speaking on SEN radio in Australia, Johns said it was a "very interesting time for the English Super League".

"You've got a situation, Mary Fowler, who is [Nathan's] partner, she plays for Manchester City - he's already been offered a million pounds by Hull.

"If the NRL does take over, and they're looking to push the game into London... it might be in the NRL's best interest to have Nathan Cleary go to the London Broncos."

Nathan and Ivan Cleary after the winning 2024 NRL Grand Final AAP/www.photosport.nz

Reuniting the family?

Younger brother Jett has been an early release from his contract with the Warriors on compassionate grounds, allowing him to return to Australia to reunite with Nathan and father Ivan at the end of the 2026 season.

At one stage, Jett appeared to be in contention for a potential first-grade Warriors debut, but that has yet to happen.

And with just a few rounds remaining in the regular season, that prospect now looks even less likely, with coach Andrew Webster appearing to favour other options.

It would take rookie Luke Hanson or halves partner Chanel Harris-Tavita going down with a serious injury this weekend for Jett to make any kind of first-grade debut at the Wahs, making him the fifth (potentially sixth, behind Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad) option as backup halfback for the team.

Jett Cleary has been granted an early release from his Warriors contract. Andrew Cornaga/Photosport

Warriors general manager recruitment, pathways and development Andrew McFadden said while the club wanted Jett to stay, they ultimately accepted his reasons for "wanting to go home".

The Daily Telegraph had reported Jett had expressed his desire to return to the Panthers to be coached by Ivan for his final season in charge.

Speaking on NRL 360, league reporter Michael Carayannis said "it's all based on the fact that Ivan has one season left in charge of the Panthers and Jett would like to be coached by his dad in an NRL set-up for the final time"

So could Nathan extend his time at Penrith for a year, to play alongside his brother?

World.title: How immigration has been used to win votes in New Zealand elections
World.content:
New Zealand First leader Winston Peters attracted a firestorm of criticism last month after telling China-born Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan to "go back to where you've come from" during a tirade in Parliament.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon called the remarks racist, with other party leaders calling for Peters to lose his foreign affairs portfolio.

Amid calls for an apology, Peters argued his conduct was justified given Xu-Nan's heckling during his speech in Parliament.

However, Luxon pointed to another reason Peters made the comments, suggesting the foreign minister was "playing a game" to attract voters ahead of the November election.

Luxon expressed confidence in his foreign minister but noted that "the reality is we're now in full-blown campaign mode".

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters told China-born Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan to "go back to where you've come from" in response to heckling in Parliament in July. RNZ

Immigration has already been deployed by a New Zealand First MP in the lead-up to the election.

In April, New Zealand First deputy leader Shane Jones compared the country's free trade deal with India to a "butter chicken tsunami".

New Zealand First opposes the trade deal.

The country's Indian community called Jones' remarks "distasteful", with some suggesting the rhetoric was linked to the upcoming election.

Indeed, the latest remarks from Peters and Jones on immigration follow similar patterns that have been part of the country's election cycles in varying degrees since 1987, when the Immigration Act was introduced to remove racial and national discrimination.

Victoria University historian Sekhar Bandyopadhyay highlighted these patterns in an RNZ interview in July, saying that "migration has always been an issue in every election, with this year being no exception".

A man is taken away during a dawn raid in the 20th century. Supplied by Vaafusaga Tupuola Masunu Tuisila

Blame games begin

New Zealand has a well-documented history of racism against Chinese, Indian and Māori communities in the early 20th century.

However, such attacks weren't typically part of an election cycle.

This changed in the 1970s after a series of dawn raids were carried out by successive Labour and National governments during the era.

At the time, the country faced unprecedented hardship due to factors such as global oil shocks and the United Kingdom entering the European Economic Community, which ended New Zealand's preferential access to its market.

Cost of living increases and rising unemployment became election issues in 1975 and attitudes towards immigration hardened.

National Party leader Robert Muldoon, who was in opposition at the time, adopted a hardline stance on immigration, running controversial television s that depicted Pacific Islanders in a negative light as a drain on economy and social services.

Muldoon won the election by a landslide and remained prime minister until 1984, when David Lange secured a win for Labour.

Prime Minister David Lange visited India during his first overseas tour after taking office, meeting Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in 1984. Archives New Zealand - Te Rua Mahara o te Kāwanatanga

Immigration reform

It was Lange who introduced the Immigration Act three years later, which saw New Zealand moving away from migration predominantly from traditional countries such as Britain and Ireland to anyone based on merit.

According to New Zealand encyclopaedia Te Ara, the legislation "marked a real break with the earlier emphasis on nationality and ethnic origin as the basis for admitting immigrants".

"Any person who met specified educational, business, professional, age or asset requirements was to be admitted, regardless of race or nationality," Te Ara says.

Four years later, the Immigration Amendment Act replaced the occupational priority list with a points system, which were awarded for employability, age, educational qualifications and available funds.

A modest level of English was also required.

These policy changes led to an increased influx of migrants from Asia.

Census data shows the country's Asian population increased at least three times between 1986 and 1996, with immigrants relocating from Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea, Japan, China and India.

In 1993, Winston Peters founded New Zealand First after leaving the National Party.

By the time the country faced its first election under Mixed Member Proportional representation in 1996, public anxiety over the changing demographics had reached a crescendo.

According to Te Ara, several groups were formed to oppose immigration from Asia.

"In 1993, Auckland community newspapers published articles by journalists Pat Booth and Yvonne Martin on the 'Inv-Asian'," Te Ara says.

"There was concern about a range of issues - everything from the driving abilities of Asians to the impact of non-English speakers on schools. Much public comment echoed the 'yellow peril' concerns of a century earlier."

RNZ

Peters campaigned heavily against high migration levels and "non-traditional" immigrants.

Critics have accused Peters of stroking fear surrounding "Asian invasion" at the time, something distinguished professor emeritus Paul Spoonley alluded to on RNZ's The Detail in May.

"If you look at that electoral cycle and the way in which migrants and migration is politicised, then we have quite a history," Spoonley said.

"You can go back to the 1970s: 1973 the overstayers campaign; the 1996 election which saw New Zealand First arrive in Parliament on an anti-immigrant but mainly an anti-Asian immigrant position."

In his defense, Peters has maintained he was only advocating for a "well-planned and managed immigration policy over the short to long term".

Indeed, some years later in 2002, Peters told a predominantly Chinese audience in Auckland that "no New Zealand First immigration policy has ever been anti-Asian, or anti-Chinese or anti any race".

"Immigration is not about race, it is about the number of migrants that New Zealand can reasonably sustain," Peters said.

Nevertheless, New Zealand First secured 13.4 percent of votes in the 1996 election, putting Peters in the kingmaker role for the first time.

Fluctuating fortunes

Over the next few election cycles, anti-immigrant sentiment took a backseat as New Zealand First's electoral fortunes fluctuated.

Support for the party plummeted to just over 4 percent party vote in 1999, before rebounding significantly in 2002 to more than 10 percent.

In 2004, National Party leader Don Brash delivered a speech in Orewa in which he decried what he saw as the special status given to Māori.

National Party leader Don Brash has mud thrown at him by a protester in 2004 a few days after his controversial speech at Orewa. teara.govt.nz

Although his remarks were not aimed at immigrants per se, the speech once again brought the issue of national identity and social cohesion to the forefront of politics.

And as New Zealand counted down to the 2005 election, Peters again made Asian immigration central to his election campaign.

He called New Zealand the "last Asian colony" in a statement to media in April 2005.

"The government's lax immigration laws are changing the face of our country forever," he said.

"Statistics New Zealand's figures demonstrate a huge demographic change with social and cultural implications which will echo through the centuries ahead.

"At this rate, it won't take long for New Zealand to be unrecognisable."

Peters stressed his concern was not about racism or bigotry, but about the impact of mass immigration on a small nation in the South Pacific.

Almost a decade later, in 2014, Peters riffed off the phrase "two wrongs don't make a right" when launching his election campaign, targeting Chinese buyers in an attack on the government's foreign land ownership policy.

The comment was widely condemned but Peters dismissed the criticism, describing the remark as a joke.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters speaks to supporters in September 2014. Winston Peters

Immigration push

After John Key became prime minister in 2008, the country's annual net migration was just 4700.

Key maintained a largely pro-immigration stance for the next eight years and, as a result, the country saw record migration - so much so that annual net migration eventually exceeded 72,500 in July 2017.

In 2016, Key acknowledged that high levels of immigration were straining the country's infrastructure, but migrants were needed to fill even simple jobs.

Prime Minister John Key met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing in March 2016. AFP

Opposition parties Labour and New Zealand First both promised to cut immigration numbers drastically in the lead-up to the 2017 election.

Labour under Jacinda Ardern vowed to reduce net migration to 20,000-30,000 a year, while New Zealand First wanted to see the number drop below 10,000.

By 2017, the narrative around immigration had changed.

Politicians were more likely to debate the sustainable number of migrants that were needed in New Zealand instead of opposing migration completely.

In August, Ardern told RNZ she felt "uncomfortable" with her Labour colleague Phil Twyford's claims two years earlier that overseas Chinese buyers had pushed up Auckland house prices, eventually apologising to anyone offended by the controversy.

In 2018, Twyford expressed regret for the incident.

Labour MP Phil Twyford expressed regret in 2018 for saying that overseas Chinese buyers had pushed up Auckland house prices. RNZ

Border closures

The 2020 election coincided with the country going through various cycles of border closures and lockdowns.

Immigration was no longer a top-tier issue, and political parties were waiting for borders to reopen to form their immigration policies.

As borders reopened in the latter half of 2022, the Labour government introduced an accredited employer work visa scheme to bring in workers to support the struggling economy.

More than 80,000 accredited employer work visas were issued within a year before reports started indicating a significant uptick in cases of migrant exploitation.

National, ACT and Labour all announced similar immigration policies targeting migrant parents and grandparents ahead of the 2023 election, with Labour also promising an amnesty for overstayers who have been in the country for 10 years or more.

A growing number of New Zealanders view Asia as being important to the country's future. RNZ / Ruth Kuo

Growing importance of Asia

The latest Ipsos Issues Monitor, which surveyed around 1000 New Zealanders on the most pressing issues facing the country in July, ranked immigration as the 11th most important priority.

Cost of living, healthcare, economy, housing and unemployment led the list, with just 8 percent of those surveyed identifying immigration as an issue.

However, this hasn't stopped some politicians dragging immigration into the election cycle, with individuals of Indian and Chinese heritage bearing the brunt of attacks.

The recent signing of a free trade deal with India - which Peters has called "far too generous", particularly on immigration - hasn't helped either.

Importantly, though, a growing number of New Zealanders are continuing to view Asia as being important to the country's future.

The Perceptions of Asia and Asian Peoples survey in June found 81 percent of New Zealanders believed that developing ties with Asia is important.

New Zealanders were also feeling more connected to Asia than ever, the survey said, with food, travel and entertainment viewed as key avenues for engagement.

World.title: Police investigate Far North death
World.content:
Police are making enquiries following a death in the Far North.

Emergency services were called to a property in Haruru around 4.30am Saturday, where a person was unresponsive.

They were pronounced dead a short time later.

A scene guard is currently in place, and enquiries are underway to determine the circumstances of the death.

World.title: Country Life: Taranaki dairy farm's herd home
World.content:
Bordering the national park that surrounds Taranaki Maunga, Crystal Rivers Farm takes its name from the many waterways which radiate out along its paddocks.

It's nestled in a part of the region prone to high rainfall, where big storms can bring over 200 millimetres of rain in just a few days.

As such, it's a hard place to winter dairy cows without running the risk of runoff and paddock sediment making its way into the waterways.

It's why Paul Kuriger made the decision to spend a little more money when buying into the 194-hectare farm and investing in a herd home.

Herd home: How a Taranaki dairy farm lifted its milk solids by 30,000 kilograms Country Life Download MP3 10m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

What is a herd home you ask?

Well it's a type of covered shelter used on dairy farms where cows have the freedom to move around and rest in a large open area that has a roof.

"We didn't want to contribute sediment throughout the winter and run off into the streams. We're always looking at winter grazing and winter grazing bills were always going up and up and up," Kuriger said.

"So we thought at the time, we would take an extra $500,000 out, spend that capital on putting a barn on so it could have greater uses than just grazing off-farm as it could be used for calving as well."

Named Crystal Rivers, water quality is certainly a key focus for the Taranaki farm which is run by Paul Kuriger. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The 4400m2 barn can fit up to 400 cows. But with only 360 cows in the herd, that's about 12m2 per cow on a soft bed of wood chips and cows enjoying about 11 kilograms of dry matter - hay or silage - each day.

Kuriger told Country Life it had been a great investment and allowed him to increase milk production by an extra 30,000 kilograms of milk solids each year.

That's because it allows the farm to keep milking for an extra month, with the cows taking shelter and being fed from inside the barn between May and October.

The 4400m2 barn can fit up to 400 cows - at its current lower stocking rate that's about 12m2 per cow, on a soft bed of wood chips. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The cows average 11 to 15 full days in the barn over the winter months, but Kuriger prefers they have the freedom to come and go from the shelter to the paddock.

"I've had the cows in here when we've had 8 inches of snow on the ground outside, and I've even opened the gate at the other end of the barn, and all I've had is a cheeky heifer walk out and then spin around and run back inside."

Kuriger said it had also helped cut down feed wastage as it prevents hay and silage being pushed into the ground and not utilised. It means they can save the pasture for when it's needed.

"With the utilisation of the feed in the barn, you're finding in some senses you're actually feeding less because the cows do so well.

"They're contented. They're quite happy in here. They're not battling the elements."

He said the animal welfare benefits had been huge.

The farm borders the national park around Taranaki maunga from which many waterways radiate out. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

In the spring, two weeks before calving starts, he'll move the cows to the shed where they stay until they've calved - offering the best possible start for the newborns.

"[We have] very few calf losses because it's just they're born into a temperature of probably 24, 25 degrees when all the cows are in the barn. So those calves are up and running straight away."

The wood chip base provides another benefit - it's eventually taken out and spread across up to a third of the paddocks on farm as a fertiliser.

All of the farm's waterways have been fully fenced off, and about 36-hectares of the almost 200-ha property are covered in native bush. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

All of the farm's waterways have been fully fenced off, and about 36ha are covered in native bush which also helps with ensuring the waters of the farm run crystal clear.

At an existing wetland Kuriger pointed out how the stock set backs had been pushed further out, allowing him to infill the border with more native plants.

He told Country Life these helped to filter water from big rainfall events before it made its way into the stream.

"Before it actually enters the inner half stream, which is right beside it, the water [will] turn a bit brown, and then it will clear itself up a day or so after the event, and the sediment will sit in the pond in the base of the pond, and it keeps returning clear water back to the stream.

"With the bush filtering it, it's a great advantage and it's a great asset for the farm."

World.title: Protesters interrupt ACT's South Island campaign launch
World.content:
Protesters received short shrift from ACT party faithful at its South Island campaign launch on Friday night.

There had been tight security at the Christchurch Town Hall, with bag searches for the hundreds of attendees and several people pre-emptively removed before the speeches began.

Three women calling for sanctions on Israel disrupted party leader David Seymour's speech, but were drowned out by jeers from the crowd.

The event comes days after a National Party public meeting in the city was disrupted around half a dozen times by people protesting Israel's wars in the Middle East, mining on the West Coast and southern data centres.

The ACT party had been announcing its proposal for of a national cancer centre, receiving a positive response at the event.

ACT party supporters argue with pro-Palestine supporters outside Christchurch’s Town Hall. RNZ/Keiller MacDuff

ACT list candidate Paul Henry publicly raised the idea as an off-the-cuff remark and said he expected to be chastised.

But he told the crowd at the launch the party has now adopted the policy, and will build the $2 billion centre if re-elected in November.

World.title: Argentina star hit with one of the biggest bans in World Cup history
World.content:
FIFA banned three Argentina players overnight, including a 10-match suspension for midfielder Leandro Paredes, for striking Spain opponents after losing the World Cup final.

The ban for Paredes — who grabbed Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat and pushed Gavi to the ground — ranks with the FIFA sanctions for Uruguay forward Luis Suárez in 2014 as among the most severe in World Cup history.

Argentina defender Nahuel Molina was handed a seven-game ban while Thiago Almada was given a one-game suspension. FIFA imposed fines of $US90,000 ($AU125,000) on Paredes and Molina, and $US30,000 for Almada.

The ban for Paredes is effectively a one-year expulsion from the Argentina team as the FIFA calendar for national team schedules includes 10 games through June 2027.

All of those games could be friendlies with no competitive games currently scheduled.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina is confronted by Spanish captain Rodri after the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Martin Rickett/PA Images)

Gavi also was banned for one game, which is a Nations League match for Spain against England at Wembley on September 26.

An Argentina coach, Roberto Ayala, was also handed a three-game ban and a $US30,000 fine.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) was fined $US110,000 for a range of incidents during the World Cup, including players carrying a political banner about the Falkland Islands after the semifinal win against England, and discriminatory chants by fans.

AFA was also ordered by FIFA to spend $US100,000 on anti-racism projects. Argentina received $US34 million in World Cup prize money from FIFA.

AFA can appeal the longer sanctions and fines to FIFA, and likely after at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

"The AFA legal department will, in a timely manner, request from FIFA the grounds for the reviewable rulings in order to file appeals with the governing body's appeal committee, while retaining the future option of appealing to the CAS as a final recourse," the federation said in a statement.

Luis Suárez holds his teeth after biting Italy's Giorgio Chiellini. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

In 2014, Suárez was banned from all soccer for four months, including for his new club Barcelona, and eight more competition games for Uruguay for biting Italian defender Giorgio Chiellini in a World Cup group stage game in Brazil.

Paredes' 10-game ban equals that in 2013 for Josip Simunic of Croatia after winning a World Cup qualifying play-off. Simunic used a megaphone to lead fans chanting a slogan used by the country's pro-Nazi regime during World War II.

The on-field clashes at last month's final in East Rutherford, New Jersey — which were charged by FIFA as assault cases — came after Argentina lost a testy final to Spain where the team was mostly outplayed and barely created a scoring chance.

Spain forward Ferran Torres scored the only goal in the second period of extra time, after Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez was sent off.

FIFA disciplinary judges also ordered Argentina to play its next home game in a stadium limited to 50 per cent of capacity. FIFA deferred a second stadium sanction and a $US100,000 fine for probationary periods.

World.title: Wildcard woes: Why the Crows are walking a tightrope
World.content:
The weight of expectation can be a relentless burden.

For a success starved fanbase it can fuel volatility and in a two-team town it's a pressure cooker.

On the eve of finals, the Adelaide Crows find themselves walking a wildcard tightrope.

If the Lions, Hawks, Demons or Cats fail to lose their final round match-ups, which they are heavily favoured to win, the Crows would have to face Carlton or the Western Bulldogs in a sudden death showdown that 12 months ago didn't even exist.

Since the AFL expanded to 18 sides, a 15-win season guaranteed you a Top 6 finish in 11 of the 13 full length seasons and only twice locked in an away elimination final.

Now even if Adelaide beats GWS on Saturday night, it could still face the precarious possibility of being both the first minor premier in the AFL to exit in straight sets and the first ever side to lose a wildcard final.

It's a situation that will only amplify an emotional fanbase that is losing faith in its game plan and direction; often questioning selection and coaching online after results.

Adelaide's success starved fanbase make their opinions known. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Adelaide Head of Football Adam Kelly addressed their behaviour a month ago on SA Grandstand stating their performances were being exaggerated.

"Our game certainly stacks up. We've had some terrific wins and some disappointing losses but there are very few teams who don't have that," he said.

" Adelaide is a very noisy place. We just need to make sure we stay focused on what's important and stay grounded and realistic about where our game is at. "

Some pundits, including 4x Showdown Medallist Josh Francou, feel anything less than a preliminary final appearance would be a failed season.

"Based on last year and the list they've got, if I'm an Adelaide supporter and I'm not playing in a preliminary final that's a fail to me. You can't win a premiership from a wildcard," he said.

"I still have a lot of question marks over Adelaide. I can't work out what's happening off field with selection and they're the number one pressure team but when sides apply pressure to them they can't handle it."

Adelaide's AFL finals drought is over With a cohesive and suffocating defence, the Adelaide Crows have the tools to put the ghosts of 2017 behind them and reach the top of the AFL mountain.

Meanwhile, others believe a strong season doesn't always lead into another. Premiership winning Crow Rod Jameson foreshadowed this after Adelaide's qualifying final loss to Collingwood last year.

"It doesn't guarantee you'll play finals again next year. If they get a couple of key injuries and drop the odd game, they'll be under enormous pressure," he predicted.

The reality is winning a minor premiership guarantees nothing but a coin flip. Only 54 per cent of winners in the AFL era have gone on to secure a premiership within three years.

Is Nicks the man?

Unfortunately Crows fans are conditioned to a ruthless pursuit of success with Matthew Nicks the first coach in their history to survive three seasons without finals.

In the past, the club has been swift in its desire to bring a fresh voice in when momentum dwindled. Now it's headstrong in its pursuit of culture and firm in its belief Nicks is their man, extending him until the end of 2027 in December.

Matthew Nicks (left) has been Adelaide's coach since 2019. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Crows president John Olsen told ABC Sport ahead of their Round 13 clash with Geelong that the club was close to breaking its near 30-year drought.

"We are united in the view that we are nearly there," he said.

"We accept we have to take it up another gear with consistency but we're not far off the pace."

"Over my six years at the club I've seen impatient fans … sustained success is what every club wants to achieve. That means you have to be deliberate, focused and disciplined in how you go about attracting talent to the club."

Selection on the ground

Adelaide's underwhelming campaign can be attributed to numerous factors.

Availability of star players was a huge problem in the first half of the season.

Izak Rankine's pre-season hamstring issue and suspension meant the man who is currently the highest ranked player in the league over the last five rounds took eight weeks to be unleashed into the midfield.

Their three-time winning best and fairest winner and skipper Jordan Dawson had to take personal leave after the tragic passing of his brother.

Crows captain Jordan Dawson had to miss several matches this year. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

All-Australian forward Riley Thilthorpe's output has dropped after tweaking his back travelling to Perth whilst Darcy Fogarty's own back issue saw him miss several weeks and key defender Mark Keane's broken ankle left the side without their defensive talisman until Round 15.

Despite the adversities, honourable losses to league heavyweights created optimism that once the troops were back the Crows would rise again.

To a degree they have, winning 8 of 11 games after their bye; but questions remain over their game plan and its ability to take the club to the top of the mountain.

The introduction and reshaping of numerous rules in the off season were designed to encourage free-flowing brands of footy.

Forever a Crow, Taylor Walker remains the boy from Broken Hill Taylor Walker arrived at the Adelaide Football Club as a 75-kilogram prospect who had only ever wanted to be a footballer. More than 300 AFL games and 700 goals later, he will retire as a club great.

Most have adopted that mantra with the ladder leading Fremantle Dockers giving Adelaide a harsh lesson last Friday on ball movement ending with +248 handball metres gained and 64 per cent ball use rating to the Crows 40 per cent.

It's a common theme for Adelaide who are last in the league for handball metres gained and third last for D50 to F50 transition.

It's a style that can open you up to immense pressure leading to high turnover rates in dangerous areas with the Crows 18th for defensive half turnovers.

The positive is they've improved on last year's midfield weakness, rising from 18th in clearance differential in the final month of 2025 to 7th in 2026 and are 4th across the season for score from centre bounce differential.

The other issue facing the Crows is selection. Their use of the new fifth bench rotation is puzzling with Matthew Nicks often prioritising pinch hit ruckman Toby Murray with limited impact.

Murray is second last for time on ground percentage (54 per cent) for players who've featured over 10 times. This decision came to a head last round when Murray had just two touches in 66 minutes.

Fans will farewell Taylor Walker at the Crows v GWS match on Saturday. (AAP: Matt Turner)

Meanwhile the management of retiring veteran Taylor Walker is in the spotlight after being flown to Perth but not selected for the finals shaping clash as a result of the clubs third game in 12 days; when the team faced cellar dwellers Richmond the week prior and could've rested their 36-year-old then.

It was an issue back in May when he played against Brisbane at the Gabba and then tore his hamstring in the Showdown five days later.

The AFL has openly said wildcard wins will be treated as a finals victory; news that was music to the ears of Essendon supporters who haven't won a final in over 8,000 days.

If Adelaide wins a match-up against a 10th placed side next weekend it might be a relief inside the four walls at West Lakes but will it satisfy a rabid fanbase?

We'll find out in a week's time.

You can hear ABC Sport's call of Adelaide v GWS from 7pm CST on ABC Listen and 891 ABC Adelaide.

World.title: 'Sad and disappointed' Sinner to miss first Grand Slam in seven years
World.content:
Top-ranked Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open, unable to recover from a right knee injury that has sidelined him since winning his Wimbledon title.

Sinner beat Alexander Zverev last month for his second straight title at the All England Club, but then pulled out of the hard-court tournaments in Montreal and Cincinnati that serve as a warm-up for the US Open.

The 25-year-old Italian wrote Friday that he will not be ready when the main draw begins on August 30.

"Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year," Sinner wrote in a post on X.

"We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue. I'm obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart. I was very much looking forward to coming back and playing in the electric atmosphere in front of the great fans there."

Sinner was the 2024 US Open champion and lost to Carlos Alcaraz in last year's final.

Alcaraz posted on social media on Thursday that he would be ready to play in New York after being out of action since April because of a right wrist injury.

The rivalry between the two has dominated men's tennis in recent years, and they met in the past three Grand Slam finals in 2025. Alcaraz took the most recent one with his four-set victory in New York.

That ended Sinner's title reign after he beat Taylor Fritz in straight sets in the 2024 final.

Sinner is 44-3 with six titles this year. He had a stunning collapse at the French Open, blowing a two-set lead while struggling in the heat in his second-round match against Juan Manuel Cerundolo.

He then sat out until Wimbledon, where his victory gave him five Grand Slam titles.

It will be the first time Sinner has missed a Grand Slam tournament since making his major debut at the US Open in 2019.
